## Introduction

::: {.narration}
Interactive cells are useful when a reader would otherwise copy code into
their own session (e.g., a first experiment, a parameter to fiddle with, an exercise).
The only cost to the user is a WebAssembly download on the first run, including any
package dependencies.

Notice that you need to use different `format`s for the two
outputs and set `engine` to `knitr`. You also must install the `r-wasm/live` 
extension in the module's directory and include the `_knitr.qmd` file at the top of
the file(s). You can install various packages in the `webr.packages` list.
:::

::: {.slides-only}
-   readers can edit and run the code here
-   nothing is installed, nothing is sent to a server
:::

## An editable cell

::: {.narration}
A `{webr}` cell is an editor with a Run button. `autorun: true` in the front
matter runs each cell once on load, so the reader sees output before touching
anything.
:::

```{webr}
x <- c(3, 1, 4, 1, 5)
mean(x)
```

## A cell the reader should not edit

::: {.narration}
`edit: false` makes a cell read-only while still running in the browser, which can
be useful for setup that later cells depend on.
:::

```{webr}
#| edit: false
penguin_mass <- c(3750, 3800, 3250, 4675, 3200)
```

## An exercise

::: {.narration}
An exercise cell carries an `exercise` label, and any `.hint` or `.solution` div
that follows with the same label is attached to it. The blanks are conventionally
underscores. You can include a check cell that runs in the browser and returns a message to the user, but it is not required.
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_mean
#| caption: "Find the mean body mass"
mean(______)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_mean
#| check: true
if (!is.na(.result) && length(.result) == 1 && .result == 3735) {
  list(message = "Great work!", correct = TRUE)
} else {
  list(message = "That's incorrect.", correct = FALSE)
}
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_mean"}
The vector from the previous slide is called `penguin_mass`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_mean"}
```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_mean
#| solution: true
mean(penguin_mass)
```
:::

## Plotting with webr chunks

::: {.narration}
You can also include a plot in an exercise, and the reader can edit the code to change it. This works especially well for teaching ggplot2, where the reader can change the aesthetics or add layers to see how it affects the plot.
:::

```{webr}
#| warning: false
#| fig-height: 4
data(penguins)
ggplot(penguins) +
  aes(x = body_mass) +
  geom_histogram()
```

## Interactive cells and the slide layout

::: {.narration}
One difference from ordinary chunks: two `{r}` chunks on a slide are expanded
into an auto-animate build-up, but interactive cells are left where you put
them.
:::

```{webr}
1 + 1
```

```{webr}
2 + 2
```

## Mixing in a rendered figure

::: {.narration}
A plain `{r}` chunk is still executed at render time, so its figure is baked into
both outputs and the slide still closes after it.
:::

```{r}
plot(mtcars$wt, mtcars$mpg)
```
